The DNN model describes the dendritic structure as a hierarchical network of thin parabolic-shaped needles.
The DNN simulations of Al-4at.%-Cu alloy were performed on domains with 14 to 118 primary dendrites, much larger than the typical phase-field simulations.
For the Al-4at.%-Cu alloy, the DNN-predicted minimum stable primary dendrite arm spacings are in good agreement, within 26% on average, with the phase-field results.

For the Ti-45at.%-Al alloy, the DNN simulations capture the reduction of primary dendrite arm spacing under increasing gravity conditions, consistent with phase-field simulations and experimental data.
The DNN simulations of the Ni-based superalloy CMSX-4 were able to reproduce the oscillatory growth behavior observed experimentally using in-situ X-ray radiography.
The DNN model considers buoyant flow in the liquid phase due to solute concentration gradients, using the Boussinesq approximation.
The DNN simulations were accelerated by implementing the code in the CUDA programming language for Nvidia GPUs.
The DNN simulations of Al-4at.%-Cu alloy with g = 9.81 m/s^2 were performed on a domain of 1150 x 510 grid points, equivalent to 8.2 mm x 3.6 mm.
The DNN simulations of Ti-45at.%-Al alloy were performed on a domain of 0.5 mm x 1.14 mm, with a grid spacing of 1.75 times the steady-state tip radius.
The DNN model includes a side-branching mechanism, where new branches are periodically generated at a distance behind the dendrite tip.
